strengths: WildFeedback provides a useful NLP resource: 20,281 preference pairs in its GPT-4 version, plus three policy-generated variants, derived from feedback in real multi-turn conversations. Connecting conversational context, expressed preferences, and training pairs is a practical contribution. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-65pe66qz/call-dffc5f97ad984e4baa1a2cb62369c7c7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

Downstream utility is supported across three model families and three established benchmarks, with regenerated UltraFeedback baselines. For example, Qwen2 trained on policy-generated WildFeedback achieves 42.6% AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate, compared with 28.7% for the starting model and 38.3% for the corresponding UltraFeedback baseline.

The paper includes meaningful human checks: feedback classification is validated on 50 conversations and checklist evaluation on 200 conversations. DSAT detection achieves 83.3% precision, with agreement approaching the reported human-human agreement. The custom evaluation also explicitly separates training and test conversations and users.

The pipeline is understandable, and the public dataset link, model identifiers, detailed prompts, and SFT/DPO hyperparameters support reproduction of the core training experiments. The resource and demonstrated downstream usefulness support a Findings recommendation.
weaknesses: The experiments do not isolate the contribution of user feedback. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, conversation length, response construction, and filtering. A comparison using the same WildChat prompts with feedback removed or replaced by generic refinement instructions would distinguish feedback-specific benefits from conversational data selection and distillation. An SFT-only comparison would also clarify the value of preference optimization.

The claim that checklist evaluation more accurately reflects actual users is insufficiently validated. GPT-4 extracts the preferences, participates in response generation and filtering, and judges the resulting responses. Human validation using those checklists is helpful, but agreement is 57.14% with κ=0.372, versus 63.27% and κ=0.436 between humans. There is no corresponding human-agreement comparison without checklists or independent validation that the summaries faithfully capture the original feedback. Better checklist-conditioned scores therefore do not establish improved user satisfaction or reduced evaluator bias.

Representativeness remains limited. Only approximately 12.8% of conversations contain detected feedback, and DSAT recall is 48.4%. The custom test further selects central preferences within 70 clusters and favors tasks resembling training data. This supports evaluation on a selected population, but does not establish coverage of majority preferences, diverse users, or evolving needs. The limitations section acknowledges selection bias, while broader claims elsewhere remain overstated.

Claims of consistent and significant superiority need qualification. No confidence intervals or variation across training runs are reported, despite several small margins. Table 3 also contains exceptions: Qwen2 trained on GPT-4 WildFeedback trails its UltraFeedback counterpart on AlpacaEval LC (39.4 versus 40.6) and MT-Bench (7.60 versus 7.66). Improvements over the starting models are more convincing than universal superiority over UltraFeedback.

Exact reconstruction of the custom benchmark is less well specified than model training. Missing details include the embedding model, clustering and deduplication settings, operational definition of user identity, and hyperparameter-selection protocol. These omissions limit reproducibility of the paper's distinctive evaluation contribution.
